paragraphs: The following judgments concern the on-site installation practices of manufactured building and mobile home installers. They do not predict hiring, licensing, qualification, or income outcomes.

The core work of manufactured building and mobile home installers is to move mobile homes or manufactured buildings to owners' sites or parks and install them: check components and requirements against work orders, estimate materials and plan operations, level and secure foundations and units, seal module openings, connect and test water, electrical, gas, and other lines, install and replace doors, windows, hardware, appliances, and interior components, inspect and test operating conditions, address leaks and structural frame damage, and complete cleanup and handover.

Entirely fictional paper task (60 minutes, no installation): work order A requests installation of a mobile home on vacant land but includes no manufacturer's installation manual, foundation acceptance record, or local work authorization. Component list B shows 4 supports, with only 3 labels legible, and 2 rolls of sealing membrane without specifications or required quantities. Interface drawing C marks water, electrical, and gas connections but has no test records, responsible personnel, or signatures. You are an observer without on-site authorization and may only organize materials. Submit an A/B/C index, missing-items list, conditional procedure draft, handover personnel and evidence, and a blank test-record template. Do not guess support specifications, judge foundation compliance, or touch interfaces.

Reference deliverable: A lacks the manual, foundation acceptance, and authorization; ask the responsible person for evidence first and do not begin placement. For B, you can confirm only that 1 of the 4 support labels is illegible; isolate it pending verification. Do not judge suitability or sufficiency from counts; membrane quantities await confirmation from the manual. For C, refer water, electrical, and gas matters separately to appropriately authorized personnel, leaving test values, results, and signatures blank. The procedure draft should say: after documentation and foundation confirmation → authorized team places, secures, and rechecks the unit → seal according to the manual → authorized personnel connect and test → hand over once evidence is complete. Do not claim installation is complete or tests passed. Reflect on whether you can accurately record unknowns and stop at scope boundaries, rather than using paper performance to prove physical capacity or competence.

On this page, manufactured building and mobile home installers refers to O*NET 49-9095.00: workers who move or install mobile homes and manufactured buildings, including titles such as mobile home installer, house mover, and installation technician. Work includes checking components and requirements against work orders, estimating materials and planning operations, leveling and securing foundations and units, sealing module openings, connecting and testing water, electrical, gas, and other lines, installing and replacing doors, windows, hardware, and appliances, inspecting and testing operating conditions, addressing leaks and structural frame damage, and completing cleanup and handover. Work mainly takes place at owners' sites, mobile home parks, and outdoors. This page excludes adjacent roles such as carpenters, construction laborers, drywall and ceiling tile installers, electricians, and plumbers.

entries: Inputs: installation work orders and site plans, mobile home or manufactured building units and modules, foundations and fasteners, sealing materials and hardware, water, electrical, gas, and other lines and interfaces, component and tool lists, technical manuals and drawings, and client and work-order requirements.

Checkable outputs: positioned and secured units and foundations, sealed module openings, connected and tested water, electrical, gas, and other systems, properly installed doors, windows, hardware, and appliances, inspection and test records, leak and frame repairs, and cleanup and handover notes.

Distinguish transport preparation from on-site installation by work order: first check home type, manufacturer instructions, site, and permits → prepare component / procedure plans → position, support, and anchor under the applicable plan → connect systems, inspect, and record within authorized scope → address defects and hand over. ONet's module-opening sealing task protects the unit before transport; do not present it as a fixed next step in on-site installation. Separately verify worker qualifications for electrical, gas, and other work.

paragraphs: Key judgments: first identify the applicable home type and installation regime, then check manufacturer instructions, soil / foundation and anchoring plans, permits, and worker authorization. Pause and hand over when site conditions do not match; do not alter structural designs independently. Qualified personnel must confirm line connections and tests under the actual applicable standards.

Environment and pace: ONet surveys show prolonged standing, bending / twisting, and kneeling / crouching are common, hazardous equipment exposure is relatively frequent, and most respondents work more than 40 hours a week. Check indoor or outdoor settings, weather, and work-at-height demands by position; do not treat all installation jobs as sharing one site environment.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 49-9095.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research conclusions do not establish qualifications, licensing, wages, or employment measures for mainland China.

Check first: installation work orders and site conditions, component and tool lists, foundation and securing plans, water, electrical, gas, and other interface requirements, boundaries of work requiring licensed personnel, and safety and weather conditions.

End-to-end work: check the work order and site, plan operations, secure foundations and units, seal openings, connect and test lines, install hardware and appliances, inspect and test, and complete cleanup and handover. Do not proceed until securing or line conditions are confirmed, or begin work at height or with hazardous equipment before protective measures are in place.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers only manufactured building and mobile home installers. Carpenters make and install wooden structures; construction laborers perform general site construction; drywall and ceiling tile installers work on interior walls and ceilings; electricians handle electrical wiring; plumbers handle water, drainage, and gas piping. Their licensing and authorizations are not interchangeable with this occupation.

Carpenters make and install wooden structures and components; manufactured building and mobile home installers position and secure whole units and connect systems. Their work subjects and sites differ.

Construction laborers perform general site construction and material handling; manufactured building and mobile home installers focus on installing and commissioning mobile homes and manufactured buildings according to their process and interface requirements.

Drywall and ceiling tile installers work on interior wall and ceiling panels; manufactured building and mobile home installers handle whole-unit sealing and structural frames and do not replace specialized interior work.

Electricians handle electrical wiring and compliant connections; manufactured building and mobile home installers connect and test interfaces only within their scope. Energized work and compliant wiring must be performed by licensed electricians.
Boundaries of AI's impact on manufactured building and mobile home installers

Editorial task hypothesis: tools may assist with fictional work orders, component lists, and draft records. Ordinary email, browsers, or spreadsheets are not equivalent to generative AI. Estimates and installation instructions require checking original document versions and site conditions. No occupational adoption rates or job outcomes were obtained; AI output cannot replace anchoring design, line tests, or installation acceptance.

Occupational sources describe actual tasks and subjects: units and foundations, sealing and hardware, water, electrical, and gas interfaces, work orders, and component lists. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; wage or employment data is not used as AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: information retrieval and records may receive assistance, but adoption depends on document permissions, versions, and review. Text output cannot replace on-site securing, system connections, or acceptance.

Human control points: check work orders and site conditions, judge whether structures and securing meet standards, confirm interfaces and test results, distinguish licensed-work boundaries, implement protection before work at height or with hazardous equipment, and take responsibility for installation quality and safety.

First conduct an offline exercise with entirely fictional work orders and component lists. Write installation steps, securing and sealing plans, testing points, and escalation boundaries without relying on unverified automated estimates to replace on-site judgment. Use the A/B/C texts above only for paper checks and handover drafts; do not perform actual installation, interface connections, or testing.
Editorial hypothesis: list or record drafts may receive assistance and must be reviewed against original work orders, instructions, and drawings. Do not infer AI adoption from software skills lists.
Use actual on-site structural, securing, interface, and safety conditions as the basis, retaining human judgment and records.
Mainland China: wage evidence and industry context

Scope: National Bureau of Statistics 2025 average annual wages for construction units are {{fact:cn-construction-nonprivate-wage}} for non-private units and {{fact:cn-construction-private-wage}} for private units; the nationwide non-private figure is {{fact:cn-national-nonprivate-wage}}. Use these as context only when the actual employer belongs to that industry. They do not show that all installers mainly fall in this category, or represent an occupational median or individual business income.

Category boundary: the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security publishes enterprise compensation survey information by occupation / position, which can be used to look up construction installation pay. This page did not obtain an entry matching O*NET 49-9095.00 exactly, so it is not used as a nationwide occupational median. Refer to competent authority publications for specifics.

Insufficient evidence: no nationwide occupational median wage, reference period, or statistical scope was obtained for manufactured building and mobile home installers in mainland China. This page displays only an industry proxy labeled as such; neither proxy figures nor US figures fill the gap.
US wage and employment scope for manufactured building and mobile home installers, occupation 49-9095.00

The 2025 US nationwide median wage for this occupation is 45,990 dollars annually and 22.11 dollars hourly; original-table percentiles are listed below. Employment facts retain the older 2024—2034 version. Current ONet figures are 3,500 employed in 2025, 5%—6% growth in 2025—2035, and 300 average annual openings. Versions and coverage periods differ; do not mix older employment size with newer projections or promise individual hiring outcomes.

Wage statistical reference: the figures above are US nationwide data for occupation 49-9095.00. The median is not starting pay or individual take-home income, and percentiles are not entry or seniority levels.

How to interpret these positions: the O*NET national page publishes wage percentiles; the median is not a beginner or senior level. Employment size and above-average growth are occupational statistics and must be interpreted separately from individual opportunities.

Industry distribution is not wages: current ONet2025 shares of 40% in retail and 18% in manufacturing describe employer settings only. Industry income cannot be inferred from the nationwide occupational median. Occupational wages by industry were not obtained; the precise gap is retained.

Employment version note: older page facts are 3,100 employed in 2024 and 2024—2034 projections; current ONet figures are 3,500 employed in 2025 and 300 average annual openings in 2025—2035. Openings include growth and replacements, not current vacancies. Small statistical size does not establish individual opportunities.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can stand, bend, kneel, and crouch for long periods outdoors at sites exposed to weather; use tools under safety procedures and protect against work-at-height and hazardous equipment risks; read work orders, drawings, and component lists and plan operations; distinguish work you may perform from work requiring licensed personnel; and accept responsibility for installation quality and safety. Tools such as RIASEC can only propose hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: can read work orders, measure, and document work, follow safety and authorization boundaries, and willingly pause when weather, foundation, or interface conditions are unmet. The A/B/C paper exercise checks information verification only; it cannot prove physical tolerance or on-site installation ability.

Reasons for caution: difficulty standing or bending for long periods or working at height, unwillingness to follow safety and protection procedures strictly, poor tolerance of outdoor weather or physical demands, or a tendency to rush before securing and interfaces are confirmed.

Trial activity: using entirely fictional work orders and component lists, rehearse installation steps, securing and sealing plans, testing points, and escalation boundaries, and ask someone else to review them against the records. Use the A/B/C texts above only for paper checks and handover drafts; do not perform actual installation, interface connections, or testing.

The O*NET interest code is RC (Realistic–Conventional), emphasizing outdoor hands-on work and organizing information according to procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through actual on-site installation, safe work, and work-order verification experiences.
Type-based tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Entry pathways and capability stages

ONet's new-hire education survey for this occupation reports 59% below high school, 40% high school or equivalent, and 1% postsecondary certificate; retain that survey scope. The several days to one year of training for Job Zone1–2 is a group description, not the time needed to obtain this occupation's license. US manufactured home installation requires checking state or HUD program installation licensing, not only water, electrical, and gas qualifications.

United States: first check home type, installation location, and the state / HUD installation program. Installers in HUD-administered states must check HUD licensing; recognized state programs follow state requirements. Current 3286.205 includes experience / education, training, and examination requirements for HUD licensing; employer instruction does not automatically authorize work. No local registered apprenticeship program for this occupation was obtained, so do not claim general availability. A Chinese qualification mapping remains unestablished; check actual construction and special-operation requirements.

Education, training, certification, and licensing are different statuses. Completing training or obtaining industry certification does not automatically grant practice or special-operation qualifications. Check authorization for water, electrical, gas, and other line connections and energized or pressurized work by state and locality. Safety and compliance conclusions must follow competent authority rules.

Entry stage: practice work-order and component checks, tool use and safety protection, foundation securing and sealing, and line interface connections and testing under supervision. Learn licensed-work boundaries and retain process records.

The work sample is an A/B/C paper verification package: material index, known / unknown list, conditional procedure draft, specialist handover form, and blank test-record template, labeled fictional, with no on-site work or verification performed. Seven-day plan, 20 minutes daily: day 1, extract A/B/C facts; day 2, distinguish missing items from assumptions; day 3, list pause and handover conditions; day 4, write procedure prerequisites; day 5, prepare a blank test template; day 6, check errors against the reference deliverable; day 7, organize and reflect on the work, then look up one target employer's requirements and retain the date. If none is found, record that rather than inventing a hiring sample.

Next step: check the target employer's hiring and safety requirements, state or local licensing and special-operation rules, and tools and components used. Validate securing, connection, and testing abilities through real installation under supervision.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may handle complex units and whole-site installation, train newcomers, oversee safety and quality standards, or move into installation crew management, construction coordination, and inspection.
Market signals and transition directions

Older facts retain 3,100 employed in 2024 and 300 average annual openings in 2024—2034; current ONet figures are 3,500 employed in 2025, 5%—6% growth in 2025—2035, and 300 average annual openings. All are occupational statistics, not hiring samples. Do not substitute old and new coverage periods or interchange growth and openings.
Cumulative growth of 6%

Transferable capabilities: safety and protection procedures, work-order and drawing interpretation, measurement and securing, line interface connections and testing, tool use and maintenance, outdoor work and work at height, and on-site communication and documentation.

First target, carpenter: add layout, cutting, and joining of wooden structures / components, drawing dimensions, and carpentry quality control. Measurement and tool experience in unit installation does not automatically establish wooden-structure fabrication ability; verify safety and authorization for the target trade.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work risks and boundaries for manufactured building and mobile home installers

risks.consequence: May affect unit safety and use.
risks.mitigation: Check applicable manufacturer installation instructions and approved foundation / anchoring plans. Pause and hand over if site conditions do not match; do not alter support or structural designs independently.
risks.scenario: Foundations or securing are not completed according to procedures.

risks.consequence: May cause leaks, power loss, or injury.
risks.mitigation: Connect and test within licensing boundaries.
risks.scenario: Water, electrical, gas, or other line connections or tests are inadequate.

risks.mitigation: Implement suitable protection and training according to work category and on-site edges, openings, and hazardous equipment. Stop first when conditions are unmet; wearing a harness alone does not permit continuation.
risks.scenario: Protection is missing for work at height or with hazardous equipment.

risks.consequence: May violate safety and practice rules.
risks.mitigation: First distinguish state / HUD manufactured home installation regimes and verify installer licensing. Then separately check line-work qualifications and local permits; they cannot replace one another.
risks.scenario: Applicable installation licensing is unchecked, or specialized electrical, gas, or other work exceeds authorization.

risks.mitigation: Adjust plans for weather and pause when conditions are unmet.
risks.scenario: Unsafe construction under weather or schedule pressure.

risks.consequence: May cause rework or delivery delays.
risks.mitigation: First check and record discrepancies, then decide whether to continue or escalate.
risks.scenario: On arrival, the work order, components, or site differs from expectations.

source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against the original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 49-9095.00 Manufactured Building and Mobile Home Installers (Summary): provides occupational identity, the official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 49-9095.00. Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 49-9095.00 Tasks: provides tasks including moving and installing mobile homes or manufactured buildings, sealing module openings, connecting and testing lines, estimating materials and planning operations, installing and replacing doors, windows, hardware, and appliances, inspecting and testing operating conditions, and repairing leaks and structural frames. Task examples do not mean every position performs every task. O*NET 49-9095.00 Work Context: describes hazardous equipment exposure, prolonged standing, bending, twisting, kneeling and crouching, outdoor work in all weather, work at height, and workweeks exceeding 40 hours for most respondents. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 49-9095.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS Display): 2025 BLS OEWS median wages for this occupation. The national page publishes the 10 / 50 / 90 percentiles of 27,120 / 45,990 / 60,810 dollars / year. O*NET 49-9095.00 National Employment Trends: employment in 2024 and projections for growth and job openings in 2024—2034. Projections are not a hiring guarantee. Industries: 49-9095.00: the main industries on that page for 2024 are Retail Trade and Manufacturing. Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 49-9095.00 Education and Occupational Preparation: Job Zone 1-2; most positions require high school or below, and on-the-job training ranges from several days to one year. Education distribution does not establish mandatory requirements for every employer. Licenses & Certifications: 49-9095.00: O*NET provides state licensing and national certification lookup entry points. Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. An exposure index is not an adoption rate, job outcome, or hiring probability. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025: provides average annual wages by industry category for urban non-private and private units, including construction. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individually owned businesses and freelancers. Enterprise Compensation Survey Information (2024): the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security's enterprise compensation survey information provides a pay lookup entry point by occupation / position. Covers urban enterprises, excluding government agencies and public institutions; this page did not obtain an exact occupational match. FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Manufactured Building and Mobile Home Installers: organizes potentially assisted tasks and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussions. An editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.
